title: Chevron Strikes Oil and Gas Condensate in Angola's Lower Congo Basin
excerpt: The discovery at Block 0 encountered a 600-meter hydrocarbon column with high-quality reservoir rock, extending Chevron's infrastructure-led exploration push in sub-Saharan Africa.
body:
• Chevron discovered oil and gas condensate at an exploration well in Block 0, offshore Angola's Lower Congo Basin, encountering a hydrocarbon column exceeding 600 meters in the Pinda reservoir.
  • The well found more than 90 meters of net pay in what Chevron described as high-quality rock, signaling potentially significant recoverable volumes.
  • The discovery adds to Chevron's infrastructure-led exploration strategy in sub-Saharan Africa as U.S. shale growth tops out and international oil majors turn to West Africa for new production.
  • Angola, sub-Saharan Africa's second-largest oil producer, introduced reforms and tax cuts in late 2024 to attract investment and spur exploration in mature offshore blocks.

The Discovery

Chevron said on Monday it had discovered oil and gas condensate at an exploration well in Block 0, offshore Angola, marking a fresh success in its push to grow production in sub-Saharan Africa through infrastructure-led exploration.

The well in Angola's Lower Congo Basin encountered an oil and gas condensate column exceeding 600 meters in the Pinda reservoir, including more than 90 meters of net pay in what Chevron described as high-quality rock. The scale of the find — a 600-meter hydrocarbon column is substantial by any offshore standard — suggests the discovery could yield meaningful production volumes, though Chevron has not yet disclosed flow-test results or reserve estimates.

Block 0 is operated by Chevron subsidiary Cabinda Gulf Oil Company (CABGOC), which holds a 39.2% working interest. Sonangol EP holds 41%, TotalEnergies holds 10%, and ENI Angola Production BV holds 9.8%.

"Block 0 is operated by Chevron subsidiary Cabinda Gulf Oil Company (CABGOC), which holds a 39.2% working interest."

Why West Africa Matters Again

With growth in U.S. shale production topping out, international oil majors are turning fresh attention to West and South Africa. The continent's underexplored offshore basins — which share geological similarities with the prolific formations off Brazil's coast — hold the promise of large new discoveries.

"It just adds to a great suite of exploration blocks we have up and down the coast in West Africa, a super prolific area," Liz Schwarze, Chevron's vice president for exploration, told Reuters earlier this year.

Angola is sub-Saharan Africa's second-largest oil producer and has been working to reverse a decline in output from mature fields. In late 2024, the government introduced a presidential decree with reforms and tax cuts aimed at making mature blocks more investible and spurring exploration. The regulatory overhaul has drawn renewed interest from international operators who had been scaling back African exposure.

Chevron's Angola Footprint

Chevron has operated in Angola for more than 70 years and remains one of the country's largest international energy operators. Through CABGOC, the company operates two offshore tracts: Block 0, adjacent to the Cabinda province coastline, and deepwater Block 14.

Block 0 is one of Angola's most prolific offshore producing areas, accounting for approximately 12% of the country's daily energy output. In December 2025, Chevron achieved first oil from the South N'dola platform in Block 0 — just over two years after construction began. That platform is tied back to the Mafumeira processing facility, leveraging spare capacity in existing infrastructure for cost-effective development.

Chevron is not alone in expanding African exploration. Shell recently acquired stakes in two undeveloped offshore blocks in Angola, and the Eni-BP joint venture Azule Energy drilled the country's first gas-specific exploration well, finding potentially more than 1 trillion cubic feet of gas and up to 100 million barrels of condensate. In Namibia's Orange Basin — one of the world's hottest exploration zones — multiple operators have recorded discoveries totaling an estimated 6.2 billion barrels of oil equivalent, according to S&P Global Commodity Insights.

What to Watch

The Monday discovery extends a trend of undeveloped gas-condensate and crude oil discoveries in Block 0's Greater Vanza Longui Area that are currently undergoing appraisal. Chevron will likely conduct flow tests and appraisal drilling to determine whether the find supports a development decision.

For the global oil market, the renewed interest in West African exploration offers a potential counterweight to slowing U.S. shale growth and OPEC's ongoing production management. Whether these discoveries translate into meaningful new supply will depend on development timelines, infrastructure investment, and the fiscal terms Angola offers to make projects economic in a volatile price environment.
